item.title: IDBI Bank acquisition puts Fairfax's CSB Bank stake at a crossroads
item.description: Fairfax Financial Holdings Ltd., led by Canadian billionaire Prem Watsa, is set to acquire nearly 61 per cent stake in IDBI Bank for $5.6 billion, marking the largest foreign investment in banks ...
item.dc:creator: Subrata Panda, Aathira Varier
item.content:encoded: With Canadian billionaire Prem Watsa’s Fairfax Financial Holdings set to acquire a nearly 61 per cent stake in IDBI Bank for ₹52,878 crore ($5.6 billion), the group faces a choice between merging the lender with CSB Bank, in which it already holds a 40 per cent stake, and exiting the smaller bank. The government has set a two-year deadline for Fairfax to either merge the two lenders or divest its stake in CSB Bank.While a merger could offer synergies, integrating the two banks could be complex as they use different technology platforms. IDBI Bank uses Infosys Finacle, while CSB Bank operates on Oracle FLEXCUBE. Although the systems share some similarities, integrating in data structures, products and applications will have some cost. The government will sell a 30.48 per cent stake in IDBI Bank, while Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC) will divest 30.24 per cent, leaving them with residual stakes of 15 per cent and 19 per cent, respectively. A merger could nevertheless offer business synergies, given CSB Bank’s focus on retail banking and IDBI Bank’s presence across both retail and corporate lending, experts said. According to Dinesh Kumar Khara, former State Bank of India chairman, the conclusion of IDBI Bank’s long-pending divestment process removes a key overhang. Having cleaned up its balance sheet, IDBI Bank is geared up for growth, with fresh capital to expand lending to small and medium enterprises (SMEs) and mid-sized corporates, a segment that could offer better margins.The new ownership structure could also strengthen governance, with the incoming shareholder taking control while the government and LIC retain board representation, Khara said. The deal also underscores foreign investors’ confidence in India’s financial sector, he added. The restructuring will attract foreign banking expertise, including from G7 countries, help further modernise banking services, strengthen competition, generate employment and bring long-term foreign investment into India, according to experts.Khara said a merger between CSB Bank and IDBI Bank could create synergies, given CSB’s retail focus and IDBI’s presence in both retail and corporate lending. The decision, however, would rest with the respective boards after evaluating the options. Differences in technology platforms should not, by themselves, be a barrier to a merger, though they could lengthen the integration process, Khara said. The acquiring bank would need to align data systems, front-end applications, back-office operations and systems, he added.  Fairfax already has interests across banking, non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), capital markets and insurance. Through FIH Mauritius Investments, it held a 40 per cent stake in CSB Bank and a 26.8 per cent stake in IIFL Capital Services as of June 2026. Its stakes in 5paisa Capital and IIFL Finance stood at 24.5 per cent and 13.6 per cent, respectively, as of September 2026. Fairfax has also been reported to be exploring a sale of its entire stake in IIFL Finance, with the Canadian investor said to be in talks with global private equity players. The other option for Fairfax is to exit CSB Bank. “Fairfax is more likely to exit CSB Bank than merge it with IDBI Bank, as IDBI presents a significantly larger opportunity for the group to expand its financial services presence in India,” said Vivek Iyer, partner and financial services risk leader at Grant Thornton Bharat. Fairfax has been looking to build a much larger financial services franchise in India, and IDBI Bank’s scale makes it a strategically important opportunity, Iyer said. “While CSB Bank has delivered good returns and still offers significant upside, it is a relatively regional bank, and the synergies from combining it with IDBI may be limited, apart from a potential opportunity in the NRI business,” he said. As of June 30, 2026, IDBI Bank had a balance sheet size of ₹4.44 trillion, net advances of ₹2.58 trillion and deposits of ₹3.25 trillion. Its net worth stood at ₹59,024 crore. Retail lending accounted for 70 per cent of its gross advances, while corporate lending made up the remaining 30 per cent. In comparison, CSB Bank had a balance sheet size of ₹58,101 crore, gross advances of ₹40,867 crore and deposits of ₹45,515 crore. IDBI Bank had more than 2,000 branches, compared with 868 for CSB Bank. Iyer also flagged labour and integration challenges at IDBI Bank as potential hurdles to a merger. “IDBI already faces labour union and industrial relations challenges, and merging CSB into the bank would add significant integration complexities. Therefore, retaining CSB as an independent investment and eventually monetising the stake appears to be the more pragmatic option,” he said. The proposed IDBI acquisition could also prompt Fairfax to reassess its broader financial services exposure in India, including its investments in IIFL and IIFL Finance, particularly in light of potential regulatory considerations, Iyer said.

item.title: HDB Financial Services sees 34% profit jump to ₹780 crore in Q2FY27
item.description: HDB Financial Services reports a 34.2% rise in Q2 FY27 profit to ₹780 crore, supported by loan growth, lower provisions and improved asset quality ...
item.dc:creator: Press Trust of India
item.content:encoded: Non-banking financial company HDB Financial Services on Wednesday reported a 34.2 per cent surge in profit after tax to ₹780 crore in the September quarter of FY27 driven by higher loan demand and lower provisions.The financial services entity had earned a PAT of ₹581 crore in the year-ago period.Its net interest income rose 15.6 per cent to ₹2,534 crore in the July-September quarter of FY27, up from ₹2,192 crore in the corresponding quarter of the previous fiscal year, the firm said in a stock exchange filing.HDB Financial Services' total income rose 12 per cent to ₹3,188 crore for the quarter under review from ₹2,851 crore in the year-ago period.Loan losses and provisions declined by 2.5 per cent to ₹730 crore for the quarter ended September 30, 2026 compared to ₹748 crore recorded in the same quarter last year.The company registered a 12 per cent growth in gross loan book to ₹1.24 lakh crore during the quarter under review compared with ₹1.12 lakh crore in the year-ago period. The financial services firm's asset quality improved with Gross stage 3 loans declining to 2.43 per cent of total loans at the end of September 2026, from 2.81 per cent in the year-ago quarter.Also, net stage 3 loans fell to 1.09 per cent from 1.27 per cent. HDB Financial Services' assets under management (AUM) stood at ₹1,24,638 crore as of September 30, 2026, up 11.6 per cent from ₹1,11,721 crore a year earlier. The company's board has approved an interim dividend of ₹2 per equity share, with October 23 fixed as the record date to determine eligible shareholders.

item.title: Housing demand up 8.2% in Q2FY27 on festive cheer: Magicbricks report
item.description: Magicbricks' PropIndex report showed housing demand rose 8.2 per cent in July-September 2026, with premium homes gaining traction, though demand stayed below year-ago levels ...
item.dc:creator: Akshat Ayush
item.content:encoded: India’s residential property market witnessed an improvement in buyer sentiment with the festive season in sight as housing demand rose 8.2 per cent between July and September 2026, according to Magicbricks’ PropIndex report. Major residential markets registered an increase in demand in Q2FY27 as property prices rose marginally. However, demand remained below year-ago levels. “The latest PropIndex findings reflect strengthening demand across key residential markets, alongside growing interest in premium housing. Homebuyers continue to prioritise location, space and value, while varying supply and price trends highlight the importance of local market dynamics,” Prasun Kumar, CMO at Magicbricks, said. Homes priced above ₹3 crore recorded notable demand growth in Greater Noida, Bengaluru and Noida. Magicbricks said this pointed to continued interest in higher-value properties, while also reflecting the varied nature of buyer demand, with premium housing gaining traction alongside sustained interest in more practical home configurations. Homebuyer preferences continued to centre on mid-sized homes, the report added. Properties measuring 750–1,250 square feet (sq ft) accounted for the largest share of demand, followed by homes in the 1,250–2,000 sq ft category. Together, these segments represented more than two-thirds of overall demand. Meanwhile, two-bedroom and three-bedroom apartments remained the most preferred configurations, highlighting buyers’ focus on balancing space requirements with location and overall value. On the supply side, active property listings registered a modest increase nationally, with Bengaluru recording the strongest growth among the highlighted markets, followed by Noida and Hyderabad. In contrast, available listings contracted in Gurugram, Chennai and Ahmedabad. Magicbricks said the variation in supply trends across cities indicated that market conditions continued to differ by geography, with some markets seeing an expansion in available inventory while others remained relatively constrained. Property prices continued to rise, with Mumbai and Chennai recording some of the strongest quarterly increases, followed by Ahmedabad and Bengaluru. Prices remained relatively stable in Greater Noida and Gurugram, reflecting differing demand-supply dynamics across residential markets.

Home / World News / IMF chief urges wealthy nations to tackle rising global debt levels

IMF chief urges wealthy nations to tackle rising global debt levels That is forcing countries to make hard choices between supporting their most vulnerable people and meeting their debt repayment obligations

IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva | Image: Bloomberg

AP Bangkok 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 14 2026 | 10:08 PM IST

Listen to This Article

The head of the International Monetary Fund said Wednesday that the US and other wealthy nations need to urgently tackle mounting global debt levels that are weighing heaviest on low-income countries and straining the global financial system. IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said that while US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other US leaders recognise that the federal deficit and national debt have grown too high, just trying to grow the US economy out of its more than USD 40 trillion in national debt would not suffice. "At the fund, we believe that, growth, of course, helps, but it cannot deliver fast enough the necessary adjustments," Georgieva said at the autumn meeting of the IMF and World Bank in Bangkok.

"There is no magic," she said, noting some other measures would be needed. "You have to go in a direction of tightening that, bringing it down, bringing deficit down." Fiscal consolidation' faces challenges Rising debt levels and global inflation, partly resulting from high energy costs due to the Iran war, have pushed interest rates to multidecade highs, adding to the burdens of the world's poorest nations. Also Read

Global growth resilience premium

IMF raises India's growth forecast to 7% in FY27 on strong domestic demand

Efforts to bring debt under control with what Georgieva and other experts call "fiscal consolidation" have suffered setbacks from heavy spending during the COVID-19 pandemic and since. "Fiscal risks are rising, and a proper reaction is largely absent in many countries," said Rodrigo Valdes, director of the IMF's Fiscal Affairs Department. "And in major advanced economies, the effect of fiscal indiscipline does not stop at the border. It travels to the rest of the world."   "Among the world's poorest countries, interest payments have reached historic highs relative to revenue, and declining amounts of aid are creating gaps that some countries have been unable to finance," the IMF's latest Fiscal Monitor said.

That is forcing countries to make hard choices between supporting their most vulnerable people and meeting their debt repayment obligations. Nations need help with job creation, investment "We know that today the median developing country is going to pay, is actually today paying three times more on their interest repayments than developed countries," Alexander De Croo, former Belgian prime minister and the administrator of the United Nations Development Programme, said in an interview with The Associated Press. On average nearly 10 per cent of government spending is going to repay debt, and the combination of high prices for fuel, fertiliser and other needs, the impact of the El Nino weather phenomenon and higher borrowing costs has left many low income countries with little opportunity to recover.

"I mean, we don't see really a light at the end of the tunnel," De Croo said. Generating jobs, especially at a time when increasing use of artificial intelligence threatens to make many traditional occupations obsolete, is another top priority. More than 1.2 billion young people are expected to enter the global workforce in the next decade or so, while forecasts suggest a net creation of only 400 million new jobs. The UNDP announced this week a "Jobs for Prosperity" initiative that will work with governments, development banks such as the World Bank and private businesses to encourage investment in key job creating areas such as tourism, healthcare and food processing.

The initiative and other efforts will focus on helping countries attract investment by improving their governance and policies, while creating pipelines of "investible projects," De Croo said. "These are things that are feasible. It's been proven that you can do it in many places of the world.
